analysis.one_liner: Lets doctors who followed medical guidelines get malpractice cases delayed, reviewed by physician panels, and thrown out.
analysis.headline: H.R. 4106 was introduced on Feb 27, 2014, sent to House subcommittees, and never received a vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give doctors and other health care providers a 'safe harbor' from medical malpractice lawsuits whenever they claim they followed a clinical practice guideline written by a medical society the Health Secretary picks. If a doctor claims adherence to a guideline, the patient's case would be frozen before the fact-gathering (discovery) stage until a three-physician review panel weighs in. If the panel or the guideline favors the doctor, a judge would have to dismiss the case unless the patient can prove otherwise by 'clear and convincing' evidence — a much higher bar than usual — and a winning doctor could make the patient pay the doctor's legal fees.
analysis.who_benefits: Physicians, their practices, and malpractice insurers. A doctor who can point to a guideline would get near-automatic dismissal of malpractice suits, shielded from paying attorney fees, plus the right to move cases from state to federal court. Medical specialty societies would gain new, federally-endorsed authority as the authors of the guidelines that decide these cases.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a litigation safe harbor: if a physician alleges adherence to a designated clinical practice guideline, courts must suspend the case before discovery until an independent medical review panel finishes [S3].
If the panel finds the doctor adhered to an applicable guideline, the court must enter summary judgment for the doctor unless the patient proves otherwise by clear and convincing evidence [S3].
Defendants who prevail after a favorable panel finding can recover costs and attorneys' fees from the plaintiff [S3].
Adds a federal right of removal so malpractice defendants can move state-court cases to federal court when a federal payor like Medicare or Medicaid paid for any of the care [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients harmed by medical errors. Their cases would be delayed before they can obtain medical records and testimony through discovery, decided initially by panels of board-certified physicians approved by their own specialty societies, and dismissed under an unusually high burden of proof — and they could owe the doctor's legal fees if they lose.

drawbacks.text: Guidelines would be written and submitted by medical societies — the physician industry's own trade groups — and the review-panel members must be physicians approved by their specialty societies, so the industry sets the standard and reviews compliance with it [S3].

A case would be suspended before discovery, meaning a patient could be denied the evidence-gathering tools needed to prove a guideline was actually misapplied, and dismissal would require proving the case by clear and convincing evidence — a far higher bar than the ordinary preponderance standard [S3].
The panel's preliminary findings and a doctor's win could make an injured patient liable for the physician's attorneys' fees, discouraging even legitimate claims [S3].

Because federal payor status turns on any Medicare, Medicaid, or tax-credit payment for care, the federal review process could reach a very large share of malpractice cases, not just narrow federal questions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Doctors argue safe harbors cut defensive medicine costs and clarify standards; the bill text lists reducing defensive-medicine spending and improving quality as its purposes [S3]. But the protections run almost entirely one way: the guidelines are authored by physician societies, the reviewers are physicians approved by those same societies, the patient loses discovery before the panel reviews, the standard of proof is elevated to clear and convincing, and a losing patient can owe the doctor's fees. Patients who suffered real errors that deviated from a guideline could still sue, and doctors remain free to depart from guidelines when a patient warrants it [S3]. On balance the bill's benefits accrue to the medical-liability defense side and its costs to injured patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees, then to two subcommittees, and no committee or floor vote ever happened before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr (R-KY) introduced H.R. 4106 on Feb 27, 2014, joined by Rep. Ami Bera (D-CA), and it drew 19 cosponsors (18 Republicans, 1 Democrat) [S1] [S4].

The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary Committees on the day of introduction and then to the Health and Constitution and Civil Justice subcommittees within a month, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress [S5].
No hearings, markups, committee votes, or floor action are recorded, and the bill died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and trial lawyers keep the existing court process intact, since the bill never advanced. Physicians and malpractice insurers gained nothing, and no one's liability exposure changed because the bill never became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients and trial lawyers, whose court access stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan pair of cosponsors including a physician-legislator.

for.name: Rep. Ami Bera
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's Democratic original cosponsor, a physician in Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was 18 Republicans and 1 Democrat, so support leaned heavily Republican; no committee or floor votes were ever held, so the outcome reflects inaction rather than a recorded no vote [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would hand physician societies the authority to write the guidelines that function as the legal standard of care and would seat specialty-society-approved physicians on the review panels that screen malpractice cases [S3]. Doctors would gain a litigation safe harbor and fee-shifting against patients.
Mandatory pre-suit panel review, clear-and-convincing dismissal standards, and fee-shifting would reduce the number of claims that ever reach a payment decision.
The safe harbor and mandatory panel review extend to health care organizations and physician employees and agents, shrinking their malpractice exposure [S3].
Pre-discovery suspension, elevated proof standards, and fee-shifting would cut into contingency-fee malpractice work — the industry whose existence depends on patients' access to court.
